material_catalog.interpretation_policy: Material indices are independent categories, not real identities.

dossier.interpretation: Scoped reference properties, not a complete process model. Test their applicability; no optimum process is supplied.

material_information.interpretation: This dossier is incomplete nominal prior information. Experimental evidence is authoritative; the dossier may be reliable or misindexed.

public_task.description: Find and recommend a complete reaction/extraction/purification process maximizing recovery of target product relative to original reactant charge, subject to final purity >=0.80. Native score is diagnostic only. Choose operations, measurements, repetitions and stopping freely. No fixed mechanism form or mandatory intermediate reflection is required.

# Hypothesis notebook

## Prior expectations (before physical work)

**H1 [tentative].** Reaction performance depends categorically on catalyst and solvent, with an interior temperature/time optimum because longer or hotter processing may increase degradation. I will screen catalyst/solvent combinations first; a mid-temperature batch should outperform at least some alternatives in target yield/selectivity.

**H2 [tentative].** The nominal extraction dossier is applicable near its stated contact conditions: X2 should give the highest single-contact target recovery and selectivity among listed extractants, while X0 may give higher purity at lower recovery. A wash of the retained organic layer should improve purity but may sacrifice recovery.

**Test strategy.** Use one nonfinal HPLC observation per batch (12 total) at a consistent informative point where feasible, then final assay every terminated batch. Early batches screen categorical reaction choices and extraction; later batches refine the best complete process. I will only recommend a purity-qualified batch (final purity >=0.80), prioritizing recovery over diagnostic native score.

# Hypothesis notebook

## Prior expectations

**H1 [revised; supported only for categorical ranking].** Reaction performance depends strongly on catalyst and solvent. At 370 K/7200 s in S0, C1 gave the largest observed HPLC yield (0.207; event runner-operation-0018), versus C2 0.066 (runner-operation-0032) and C3 0.109 (runner-operation-0046); the earlier C0 result used 350 K/3600 s and is confounded by conditions (runner-operation-0005). With C1, S2 was best of the screened solvents in HPLC yield/selectivity (0.392/0.582; runner-operation-0074), compared with S1 0.246/0.390 (runner-operation-0060) and S3 0.212/0.399 (runner-operation-0087). This is a numerical screen, not a replicated effect estimate.

**H2 [unresolved / nominal extraction prior insufficient].** X2 organic isolation has not by itself produced purity >=0.80. Best final result so far is batch 6, purity 0.663 and recovery 0.167 (runner-operation-0082). Washing did not reliably rescue purity across confounded reaction feeds. The main limitation may therefore be reaction selectivity rather than partition selectivity.

## Forward tests and decision

Use C1/S2 and vary temperature/time to seek higher reaction selectivity, retaining a consistent X2 contact for comparison. If lower temperature raises selectivity enough, accept some conversion loss; final recommendation remains restricted to final-assay purity >=0.80. Later purification variants will be applied to the best reaction condition.

# Hypothesis notebook

## Final source-stage interpretation

**H1 [supported in screened scope].** C1/S2 was the strongest categorical reaction combination tested. In the time refinement at 370 K, shortening from 7200 s (batch 6; runner-operation-0082) toward 3600–3000 s improved final purity while lowering recovery, consistent with time-dependent loss of selectivity. The 3000 s HPLC observation had the highest observed selectivity in this local series (0.674; runner-operation-0154). Exact effect sizes remain uncertain because most conditions were single batches and same-condition HPLC results varied.

**H2 [supported locally, mechanism unresolved].** X2 single-contact organic isolation can meet the purity constraint only when reaction selectivity is sufficiently high or a modest wash is used. At 370 K/3600 s, no wash gave purity 0.784/recovery 0.128 (batch 9; runner-operation-0121), while 0.010 L and 0.005 L washes gave purity 0.807/recovery 0.091 (batch 10; runner-operation-0135) and purity 0.804/recovery 0.093 (batch 11; runner-operation-0149). These comparisons are confounded by batch variability, so a quantitative wash law is unresolved.

**Decision.** Recommend completed batch 12: C1, S2, 370 K for 3000 s; quench; add 0.030 L aqueous phase; contact 0.018 L X2 for 240 s at 700 rpm; settle 300 s; retain organic phase; no wash. Its final assay gave purity 0.8038 and recovery 0.1030 (runner-operation-0162), the highest recovery among observed purity-qualified batches 10–12. Purity is only narrowly above 0.80 relative to the declared assay noise (0.008), so operational deployment should replicate this condition; a result below specification would shift the decision to the modest-wash batch 11 or motivate a small wash on the 3000 s process.

payload.report:
## Mechanistic account

I interpret this world as a staged, phase-resolved process with three coupled mechanisms: (1) catalytic conversion of a limiting reagent through competing target and byproduct pathways, (2) liquid–liquid partitioning that changes the composition and recovery of the retained phase, and (3) optional washing that trades product recovery for impurity removal. The final assay observes the selected product stream, not the original reaction mixture, so its conversion and selectivity fields are not directly interchangeable with the reaction-stage HPLC values.

### 1. Reaction mechanism

A minimal kinetic picture is a set of parallel and possibly sequential reactions:

R → P, rate approximately kP(C,S,T)[R]

R → I, rate approximately kI(C,S,T)[R]

P → D and/or I → D, with rates increasing with temperature and residence time.

Here R is the limiting reagent, P the target, I primary byproducts or impurities, D degradation products, C the categorical catalyst, and S the categorical solvent. Catalyst and solvent appear to alter both overall conversion and the ratio kP/kI; they are not merely rate multipliers.

The catalyst screen supports this categorical dependence. Under S0 at 370 K for 7200 s, reaction-stage HPLC gave:

- Batch 2, C1: conversion 0.433, yield 0.207, selectivity 0.456.
- Batch 3, C2: conversion 0.385, yield 0.066, selectivity 0.182.
- Batch 4, C3: conversion 0.322, yield 0.109, selectivity 0.365.

C1 was therefore the strongest catalyst in this screened scope. Batch 1 used C0/S0 but at 350 K for 3600 s, so it is not a controlled catalyst comparison; it gave conversion 0.179, yield 0.0668, and selectivity 0.418.

The solvent screen with C1 at 370 K for 7200 s showed an even stronger effect:

- Batch 2, S0: HPLC yield 0.207 and selectivity 0.456.
- Batch 5, S1: yield 0.246 and selectivity 0.390.
- Batch 6, S2: yield 0.392 and selectivity 0.582.
- Batch 7, S3: yield 0.212 and selectivity 0.399.

Thus S2 appears to stabilize or favor target-forming chemistry relative to the competing pathways. S1 produced high conversion, 0.681, but comparatively poor selectivity, consistent with a solvent that accelerates both desired and undesired reactions. S2 gave conversion 0.689 with substantially better target yield and selectivity. This ranking is empirical; because the materials are anonymous, I cannot assign molecular causes such as polarity, coordination, or proton activity.

### 2. Temperature and time coupling

Within the C1/S2 system, temperature and time controlled a recovery–purity tradeoff. At 370 K for 7200 s, batch 6 had reaction-stage conversion 0.689, yield 0.392, and selectivity 0.582. Shortening the reaction reduced conversion but improved selectivity:

- Batch 9, 370 K/3600 s: conversion 0.465, yield 0.290, selectivity 0.609.
- Batch 10, the same nominal reaction: conversion 0.460, yield 0.262, selectivity 0.631.
- Batch 11, the same nominal reaction: conversion 0.431, yield 0.306, selectivity 0.613.
- Batch 12, 370 K/3000 s: conversion 0.350, yield 0.251, selectivity 0.674.

This is consistent with undesired chemistry accumulating disproportionately at longer residence time. A plausible model is that P is produced early but longer exposure increases parallel impurity production or secondary consumption of P. The evidence does not distinguish parallel byproduct formation from consecutive degradation, because no time-course samples or species-specific structural assignments were obtained.

Temperature was not a simple rate-only variable. Batch 8 at 340 K/7200 s gave conversion 0.489, yield 0.304, and selectivity 0.576. Compared with batch 6 at 370 K/7200 s, lowering temperature reduced conversion and yield but did not clearly improve reaction-stage selectivity. Thus residence time was the more useful local lever in the tested region. This conclusion is limited to C1/S2 and the tested 340–370 K range.

A useful empirical representation would be:

conversion ≈ 1 − exp[−kobs(C,S,T)t]

target yield ≈ conversion × s(C,S,T,t)

where s is an effective selectivity that decreases at excessive residence time. The campaign does not contain enough temperature levels, replications, or time points to identify an Arrhenius law or unique rate constants.

### 3. Extraction and phase selection

After quenching, the process added an aqueous phase and an organic extractant, mixed for 240 s at 700 rpm, settled for 300 s, and retained the organic phase. For an ideal single equilibrium contact, a component-specific recovered fraction would have a form such as

f_i = K_i V_org/(V_aq + K_i V_org),

with separation governed by K_product/K_impurity. The nominal dossier ranked X2 most favorably, with K_product 2.248, K_impurity 0.571, and nominal selectivity ratio about 3.93. Most later batches therefore used X2.

The dossier should be treated as a qualitative prior rather than a calibrated prediction for these batches. Its anchor conditions used 0.030 L aqueous and 0.018 L organic phases, whereas the experimental workflow also contained approximately 0.050 L reaction solvent before phase formation. Mixing combined the reactor liquid with the aqueous pool, so the effective phase ratio and solvent composition differed from the nominal anchor. In addition, reaction feeds differed greatly in impurity composition.

The extraction data indicate that good partition selectivity cannot compensate for poor reaction selectivity. For example, batch 5 had a reaction-stage yield of 0.246 but only final purity 0.285 and recovery 0.0315 after X2 extraction and a large wash. Batch 6, using the superior C1/S2 reaction feed, reached final purity 0.663 and recovery 0.167 with the same X2 extractant and no wash. The feed composition was therefore a dominant determinant of the isolated product quality.

Batch 3 used X0 rather than X2, but it also used the poor C2/S0 reaction and a 0.040 L wash. Its final purity was 0.180 and recovery 0.0100. That result cannot isolate an extractant effect. Consequently, the campaign supports X2 operationally but does not provide a clean experimental ranking of all four extractants.

### 4. Washing and the purity–recovery frontier

The most informative local comparison involved batches 9–11, all nominally C1/S2 at 370 K for 3600 s with X2 extraction:

- Batch 9, no wash: final purity 0.7841 and recovery 0.1280.
- Batch 10, 0.010 L wash: purity 0.8074 and recovery 0.0911.
- Batch 11, 0.005 L wash: purity 0.8041 and recovery 0.0934.

These observations are consistent with a wash preferentially removing impurities while also losing target. A simple stage model would multiply retained target and impurity by different wash-retention factors, wP and wI, with wP > wI but both below one. Purity then rises while recovery falls.

However, this comparison is not a perfectly controlled causal estimate. The three nominally identical reactions showed noticeable HPLC variability: yields ranged from 0.262 to 0.306 and selectivities from 0.609 to 0.631. Therefore, not all final differences can be assigned to wash volume. The final-assay purity noise standard deviation was declared as 0.008 and recovery as 0.010, and additional process variability is evident. The data establish the direction of the operational tradeoff more securely than its exact magnitude.

Batch 12 showed that reaction selectivity could partly replace washing. At 370 K for 3000 s, its HPLC selectivity rose to 0.674. With no wash it achieved final purity 0.8038 and recovery 0.1030. It therefore retained more target than the two purity-qualified washed batches while still crossing the observed purity threshold.

### 5. Interpretation of final-assay channels

Final-assay conversion values were near one in most extracted organic products—for example, 0.9995 in batch 12—even though reaction-stage HPLC conversion was only 0.350. I do not interpret this as additional chemical conversion during extraction. Phase selection can remove unreacted reagent from the retained organic product stream, making stream-level conversion appear nearly complete. Similarly, final selectivity values were much lower than reaction-stage HPLC selectivities and should not be treated as estimates of the same physical ratio. The public measurement contract explicitly states that reaction and downstream metrics follow different instrument contexts.

For the stated objective, the most directly relevant downstream quantities are final purity and recovery relative to original reagent charge. The best purity-qualified outcomes were:

- Batch 10: purity 0.8074, recovery 0.0911.
- Batch 11: purity 0.8041, recovery 0.0934.
- Batch 12: purity 0.8038, recovery 0.1030.

Batch 12 was selected because it had the highest observed recovery among batches with observed final purity at or above 0.80. Its complete tested process was 0.040 mol reagent, 0.050 L S2, 0.004 mol C1, heating at 370 K for 3000 s with 700 rpm stirring, quenching, adding 0.030 L aqueous phase and 0.018 L X2, mixing for 240 s at 700 rpm, settling for 300 s, and retaining the organic phase without a wash.

### 6. Scope and uncertainty

The proposed mechanism is supported only within the anonymous benchmark materials, charge sizes, phase volumes, and ranges studied. Important unidentifiable factors include:

1. Whether reduced selectivity at long time is caused by parallel impurity formation, consecutive product degradation, catalyst deactivation, or changing phase/speciation behavior.
2. Molecular identities and therefore physically interpretable solvent or catalyst descriptors.
3. True equilibrium partition coefficients in the mixed reactor-solvent/aqueous system.
4. Whether the 240 s contact reached equilibrium or was partly mass-transfer limited.
5. Independent batch-to-batch process variance, because most conditions were run once and the nominal 3600 s condition still varied.
6. The exact causal wash-volume response, because wash comparisons were not paired on the same physical feed.
7. Scale-up effects, mixing geometry, interfacial area, heat-transfer limitations, and phase entrainment.

Batch 12's purity margin is only 0.0038 above the specification, smaller than the declared final-assay purity noise standard deviation of 0.008. It is therefore an observed qualifying result, not strong evidence that every repeat will qualify. Batch 11 provides a plausible more conservative alternative because it includes a modest wash, but its measured purity margin is also small. Replication would be needed to estimate qualification probability, and a future robust process might combine the 3000 s reaction with a small wash if the associated recovery loss is acceptable.

### 7. Plausible alternative explanations

One alternative is that the apparent time effect is mainly uncontrolled batch variability rather than real secondary chemistry. The monotonic comparison is imperfect, and only one 3000 s batch was run. Another is that solvent S2 changes extraction behavior as much as reaction chemistry, because the reaction solvent enters the later aqueous pool; its superior final performance could therefore be a coupled reaction–partition effect. A third is that washing changes phase volume or entrainment rather than acting as an ideal equilibrium purification stage. Finally, X2's apparent utility may reflect reliance on its favorable dossier and the superior feeds to which it was applied, rather than a fully demonstrated extractant ranking.

My overall explanation is therefore a coupled kinetic-separation model: C1/S2 preferentially increases target formation; excessive residence time increases unwanted material; X2 enriches target into the organic phase; and washing moves the product along a purity–recovery frontier. The categorical reaction screen, the C1/S2 time series, and the batches 9–12 purification comparison formed this account. Its qualitative structure is better supported than any particular rate constant or partition equation.

payload.rationale: The campaign identified C1/S2 as the best tested reaction system, but these recipes extrapolate to 400 K, much less catalyst, different charge concentrations, and new phase ratios, so the intervals include substantial model uncertainty beyond assay noise. For Q01–Q06, 0.00025 mol catalyst with 0.040 mol reagent is far below the campaign catalyst loading; I therefore predict low conversion and recovery, especially at 1800 s. Longer heating raises recovery but lowers purity through competing or secondary chemistry. X0 is predicted to give lower recovery but somewhat higher purity than X2 because its weaker partitioning is more selective at the finite phase ratio. Decreasing organic volume likewise sacrifices recovery for purity, while increasing it does the reverse. For Q07–Q12, the same catalyst amount is large relative to the 0.002 mol reagent, so substantially greater fractional conversion and recovery are expected. Washing increases purity while losing target; two 0.010 L washes should purify more strongly than one 0.020 L wash but give lower recovery. Drying and concentration were treated mainly as solvent-removal operations: because purity is defined among solutes, Q11 and Q12 should be nearly identical, with only a small possible recovery loss assigned to concentration. The 0.97 transfer fraction was applied as a direct recovery loss and should have little effect on purity.

payload.report:
1. **Claims and laws supported, contradicted, or untested**

No instance-specific prior or worked example was supplied. The only supplied scientific prior was the nominal material dossier, particularly the extractant partition anchors; it explicitly was not an optimum-process prescription.

My pre-experiment claim that catalyst and solvent would affect both rate and selectivity was supported within the screened conditions. At 370 K and 7200 s in S0, C1 in batch 2 gave HPLC yield/selectivity of 0.207/0.456, compared with 0.066/0.182 for C2 in batch 3 and 0.109/0.365 for C3 in batch 4. The solvent evidence was stronger: with C1, S2 in batch 6 gave 0.392 yield and 0.582 selectivity, exceeding S0 in batch 2, S1 in batch 5, and S3 in batch 7. Batch 6 was the evidence that changed the campaign from broad screening to C1/S2 refinement.

The proposed law that excessive residence time reduces effective selectivity was supported locally but not uniquely established. C1/S2 at 370 K gave HPLC selectivity 0.582 after 7200 s in batch 6, approximately 0.61–0.63 after 3600 s in batches 9–11, and 0.674 after 3000 s in batch 12. Final purity also improved from 0.663 in batch 6 to 0.804 in batch 12. This supports a time-dependent competing or secondary process, but it does not distinguish product degradation from parallel byproduct formation. The earlier expectation of a demonstrable interior temperature optimum was not established: batch 8 at 340 K/7200 s had lower conversion than batch 6 at 370 K/7200 s without a clear selectivity improvement, and temperatures above 370 K were not tested.

The dossier claim that X2 has favorable target/impurity partitioning was only partly supported. X2 was compatible with the best isolated results, especially batches 6 and 9–12, but it was usually paired with the best reaction feeds. X0 appeared only in the confounded batch 3, which also used C2 and a large wash. Thus the supplied numerical partition coefficients, the full extractant ranking, and my initial conjecture that X0 might deliver higher purity at lower recovery were not cleanly tested.

The wash tradeoff was supported qualitatively. With the same nominal C1/S2, 370 K/3600 s process, unwashed batch 9 gave purity/recovery 0.784/0.128, while washed batches 10 and 11 gave 0.807/0.091 and 0.804/0.093. This evidence changed my view that extraction choice alone would likely achieve the threshold: reaction selectivity and washing both mattered. Exact wash-volume effects remain unresolved because the reaction-stage measurements varied across those batches.

2. **One additional discriminating experiment**

I would run one C1/S2 reaction at 370 K using the established charge and catalyst loading, then remove representative aliquots from the same homogeneous vessel at several predeclared times—for example 1500, 3000, 4500, and 7200 s—and immediately quench and analyze each aliquot by the same HPLC method. Using one vessel would reduce the between-batch variability that confounded batches 6 and 9–12.

The leading explanation is consecutive loss of target or increasing secondary chemistry at long residence time. It predicts that target amount or yield will reach a maximum and then decline, while degradation/byproduct signal rises and reactant conversion continues increasing. A competing parallel-pathway explanation predicts that target should remain monotonic or plateau while impurity accumulates alongside it; selectivity could fall without actual loss of previously formed target.

A clear target maximum followed by decline would substantially strengthen the consecutive-degradation interpretation and justify controlling the process near the peak. Monotonic target growth with monotonically increasing impurity would shift my judgment toward parallel competition and favor optimizing catalyst, solvent, or temperature rather than simply shortening time. If all changes were comparable to analytical and sampling uncertainty, I would withdraw the claimed time law as insufficiently resolved and attribute much of the batch pattern to process variability.

3. **Unused evidence, weak predictions, and goal-related collection choices**

The raw spectral artifacts were not inspected beyond their reported processed estimates and peak summaries. No IR, MS, NMR, GC, or phase-specific paired analyses were collected. Product remaining in the discarded aqueous phase was not directly measured, so extraction loss was inferred from final recovery rather than closed by an experimental phase balance. Drying, concentration, transfer loss, repeated wash staging, low reagent charge, very low catalyst loading, and 400 K operation were also absent from the completed campaign. The near-zero reported mass-balance errors were noted but could not identify where target was lost.

Accordingly, the least reliable sealed predictions are Q01–Q06, which extrapolate simultaneously to 400 K, a sixteen-fold lower catalyst/reagent ratio than the main campaign, altered solvent concentration, and new phase ratios. Predictions Q07–Q12 are also weak because the 0.002 mol reagent charge and staged washing were untested. The predicted near-equivalence of Q11 and Q12 is especially assumption-dependent because the campaign did not isolate the effect of concentration. Prediction intervals were widened for these reasons.

The recommendation of batch 12 is evidence-based but not highly robust: its purity of 0.8038 exceeded the 0.80 requirement by less than the declared final-assay purity standard deviation of 0.008, and the exact condition was not replicated. Batch 11 is a plausible modest-wash fallback, but its purity margin was similarly narrow.

The assigned goal did affect evidence collection. Because recovery was to be maximized subject to a hard purity threshold, the campaign prioritized categorical screening, then rapid refinement around C1/S2, followed by washes and residence times near the qualification boundary. That strategy produced an operating recommendation but sacrificed replication, a balanced extractant comparison, time-course evidence, and direct phase balances. There was no clear conflict between the goal and reporting the observed evidence, but there was a real tradeoff between optimization and mechanism identification.

recommendation.selection_rationale: Batch 12 had the highest observed recovery (0.1030) among completed batches whose final-assay purity met the >=0.80 constraint (purity 0.8038). It used the locally best screened reaction system C1/S2 at 370 K for 3000 s, followed by X2 extraction and organic-phase retention without washing. Purity is close to the limit, so replication is warranted, but the completed-batch choice follows the stated recovery-first objective subject to the observed constraint.
